note: Tarot archetypes are narrative labels for decision situations, not personality diagnoses.

cards.name: The Fool
cards.core_question: Will I step into the unknown?

cards.name: The Magician
cards.core_question: Can I make something happen with what I have?

cards.name: The Lovers
cards.core_question: Who or what matters most in this choice?

cards.name: The Chariot
cards.core_question: How hard will I push toward the goal?

cards.name: Strength
cards.core_question: How do I respond when emotion or pressure rises?

cards.name: The Hermit
cards.core_question: Do I need space to think before I act?

cards.name: Death
cards.core_question: When is it time to end the old and change direction?

cards.name: The Star
cards.core_question: Will I invest in a hopeful possibility?

trials.title: A New Hobby
trials.question: You have spent two years getting good at one hobby, but a completely unfamiliar hobby suddenly excites you much more. You only have enough free time to seriously pursue one. What do you do?

options.text: Jump into the new hobby and accept being a beginner again.
Keep the old hobby as your main focus while casually trying the new one.
Stay with the hobby I already know and continue building mastery.

trials.title: A Different Path
trials.question: You planned your next semester carefully, but an unexpected course outside your field looks fascinating and would force you to change the plan. What do you do?

options.text: Change the plan and take the unfamiliar course.
Make a small adjustment so I can try the course without abandoning most of my plan.
Keep the original plan because I already know it supports my goals.

trials.title: The Overseas Opportunity
trials.question: You receive a secure job offer, but also a six-month opportunity abroad doing something you have always wanted to try, with no guarantee of a job afterward. What would you choose?

options.text: Take the overseas opportunity and accept the uncertainty.
Try to negotiate a way to keep the secure option while exploring the opportunity.
Take the secure job and pursue adventurous opportunities later.

trials.title: The Blank-Slate Project
trials.question: A team offers you the choice between improving a successful existing product or joining a brand-new project with no users, no clear roadmap, and lots of freedom. What would you choose?

options.text: Join the brand-new project and help define it from scratch.
Split my effort or test the new project before fully committing.
Improve the successful product where the path is clearer.

trials.title: The Stuck Team
trials.question: Your group project is stuck and nobody knows what to do next. You have an untested idea and enough skills to build a quick prototype yourself. What do you do?

options.text: Build a quick prototype immediately and show the team what is possible.
Pitch the idea first and organize people around a small experiment.
Wait until the team agrees on a clearer plan before building.

trials.title: Limited Resources
trials.question: You want to host a small event, but you have almost no budget. You do have a room, some borrowed equipment, and friends with different skills. What do you do?

options.text: Combine whatever resources are available and create a workable version now.
Design a smaller event around the resources I can reliably coordinate.
Postpone the event until I have proper resources.

trials.title: Twenty Minutes to Fix It
trials.question: An event starts in twenty minutes and the main display system fails. You have spare laptops, cables, and several volunteers, but no official backup setup. What would you do?

options.text: Improvise a replacement system from the available equipment.
Assign people specific troubleshooting tasks and choose the best workable backup.
Simplify the event so it can run without the display system.

trials.title: No One Owns the Problem
trials.question: A useful campus service is missing, and everyone complains about it, but no organization is responsible for fixing it. What would you do?

options.text: Create a basic version myself and see whether people use it.
Recruit a few people and organize a small pilot first.
Raise the issue with an existing organization and wait for institutional support.

trials.title: The Team You Love
trials.question: You receive a great opportunity that fits your goals, but accepting it means leaving a team you genuinely enjoy working with. What do you do?

options.text: Take the opportunity because it fits my personal direction.
Look for a compromise that preserves the relationship while pursuing the opportunity.
Stay with the team because the people I work with matter more right now.

trials.title: Values vs Convenience
trials.question: Your group can choose a convenient vendor with questionable labor practices or a more expensive vendor whose practices match the group's stated values. What do you do?

options.text: Choose the values-aligned vendor even if it costs more.
Look for a compromise or gather more information before deciding.
Choose the convenient vendor because completing the project is the immediate priority.

trials.title: Friends in Conflict
trials.question: Two close friends have a serious disagreement, and both privately ask you to support their side. What would you do?

options.text: Support the person whose position best matches my own values.
Try to understand both sides and help them communicate without choosing a side immediately.
Prioritize loyalty to the friend I feel closest to.

trials.title: Dream Role, Different City
trials.question: You are offered a dream role in another city while someone very important to you cannot realistically move. What would you choose?

options.text: Take the role and accept that the relationship will have to adapt.
Search for a middle path, such as delaying, commuting, or renegotiating the role.
Turn down the role to protect the relationship and shared life.

trials.title: Twelve Hours Left
trials.question: Your hackathon prototype works, but it is mediocre. With twelve hours left, a risky feature could make it much more impressive or break the current version. What do you do?

options.text: Push hard for the risky feature and aim for a stronger final product.
Improve the existing version aggressively without risking the core functionality.
Freeze development and focus on polishing the demo and presentation.

trials.title: Behind in the Race
trials.question: You are behind your personal goal halfway through a month-long challenge. Catching up would require a much more intense schedule. What do you do?

options.text: Increase the pace and push until I am back on target.
Adjust the goal but keep steady forward momentum.
Accept the missed target and continue at a sustainable pace.

trials.title: Second Place
trials.question: You are in second place near the end of a competition. A high-risk strategy could move you into first but could also drop you far down the ranking. What would you do?

options.text: Take the risk and go for first place.
Use a moderately aggressive strategy that still protects my position.
Play safely and secure the strong finish I already have.

trials.title: One More Push
trials.question: Your team has worked for weeks and is exhausted. A major opportunity appears, but meeting it requires one final intense weekend of work. What would you do?

options.text: Rally the team and push hard for the opportunity.
Pursue the opportunity only if the team can divide the work sustainably.
Protect the team's energy and let this opportunity pass.

trials.title: Your Idea Is Challenged
trials.question: During a group discussion, someone strongly criticizes your idea and you believe they misunderstood it. What do you do?

options.text: Respond directly and firmly so my reasoning is not dismissed.
Stay calm, clarify the misunderstanding, and ask what concerns them most.
Pause the debate and return to it after everyone has had time to cool down.

trials.title: Fear Before the Stage
trials.question: You are about to present to a large audience and feel intensely nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Step on stage and use the nervous energy to push through.
Slow myself down with a short routine and then present.
Ask to reduce my role or let someone else take the most exposed part.

trials.title: A Hurtful Comment
trials.question: A friend says something in front of others that makes you uncomfortable, but you are not sure they intended to hurt you. What would you do?

options.text: Address it immediately and clearly in the moment.
Stay composed, then talk to them privately and explain how it felt.
Let it go for now unless it happens again.

trials.title: Provoked Online
trials.question: Someone publicly posts a harsh and inaccurate criticism of work you care about. What would you do?

options.text: Respond publicly and defend the work point by point.
Write a measured response that corrects the important facts without escalating the tone.
Avoid engaging publicly and focus on people who are willing to discuss it constructively.

trials.title: Everyone Already Agrees
trials.question: Everyone in your group is excited about a decision, but you still feel uncertain and have not fully thought it through. What do you do?

options.text: Join the group decision and learn from what happens.
Ask a few questions, then decide with the group if my major concerns are addressed.
Ask for time to think independently before committing.

trials.title: Too Much Advice
trials.question: You have a difficult personal decision and five friends are giving you conflicting advice. What do you do?

options.text: Choose the advice that feels most convincing and act.
Talk through the advice with one or two people I trust most.
Step away from everyone's opinions for a while and decide privately.

trials.title: Three Days to Decide
trials.question: You receive an important offer. Your friends all say to accept immediately, but the deadline is still three days away. What would you do?

options.text: Accept now because the opportunity is strong and trusted people agree.
Use the remaining time to ask targeted questions before deciding.
Spend time alone evaluating the decision before giving anyone an answer.

trials.title: The Fast-Moving Group
trials.question: A new team you just joined makes decisions very quickly in meetings, while you are still processing the information. What would you do?

options.text: Adapt to the team's pace and make decisions with the information available.
Ask the group to summarize the key tradeoffs before the decision.
Request time after the meeting to reflect before committing to important choices.

trials.title: The Project That Is Not Working
trials.question: You have invested months in a project, but the central idea clearly is not working. More revisions might save it, but there is no guarantee. What do you do?

options.text: End the current version and rebuild around a new idea.
Keep the useful parts but radically redesign the rest.
Continue improving the existing project because too much has already been invested to abandon it.

trials.title: A Familiar Routine
trials.question: A routine that once helped you is now making your days repetitive and limiting new opportunities. What do you do?

options.text: Drop the routine and design a completely new one.
Keep the best parts while replacing what no longer works.
Keep the routine because stability is still valuable.

trials.title: The Club You Have Outgrown
trials.question: You have belonged to a club for years and have many memories there, but it no longer feels meaningful or enjoyable. What would you do?

options.text: Leave and use the time for something new.
Reduce my involvement while keeping the relationships I still value.
Stay involved because the history and community still matter.

trials.title: Retiring a Successful Feature
trials.question: A product feature was once popular but now causes technical problems and serves fewer users. Removing it will upset some long-time users. What would you do?

options.text: Remove it and build a cleaner replacement for the future.
Phase it out gradually while helping users transition.
Keep maintaining it because existing users still depend on it.

trials.title: Low Odds, High Impact
trials.question: Your group can attempt a project with a low chance of success, but if it works it could genuinely help many people. What do you do?

options.text: Choose the ambitious project because the possible impact is worth the risk.
Run a small pilot first and expand only if there are promising signs.
Choose a more reliable project with a smaller but predictable benefit.

trials.title: After a Bad Semester
trials.question: After a disappointing semester, you have the chance to apply for a highly competitive opportunity you once wanted. What do you do?

options.text: Apply and treat the setback as temporary.
Apply only after making a concrete plan to improve my chances.
Focus on a more realistic opportunity until I have rebuilt confidence and experience.

trials.title: Try Again
trials.question: A friend failed at an ambitious project and now wants to try again with a revised idea. They ask you to join them. What would you do?

options.text: Join because the new attempt could still become something meaningful.
Join only if the revised plan clearly addresses what failed before.
Encourage them, but choose a more dependable project for myself.

trials.title: A Better Future, Slowly
trials.question: Your community can fund a long-term environmental project whose benefits may not be visible for many years, or use the money for an immediate improvement everyone will notice now. What would you choose?

options.text: Invest in the long-term project because future benefits are worth building toward.
Split the funding so there is both visible progress now and investment in the future.
Choose the immediate improvement because people need tangible benefits today.
